vignette:
Patient: F., a 71-year-old married woman of Middle Eastern descent
Occupation: Nanny (currently on leave)

F. arrives for her third session with a slight tremor in her hands, which she attributes to the cold, though the office is warm. She sits at the edge of the chair, her purse clutched to her chest like a shield. When she speaks, her voice is soft, careful, as though she is afraid of who might be listening.

The trauma she witnessed happened fourteen months ago, on a bright Tuesday morning. F. had been working for the same family for six years, caring for their two young children. That morning, she was pushing three-year-old Liam on the swing in their backyard. The yard faced a quiet street, a cul-de-sac where nothing ever happened. F. remembers the sound of a car engine revving, then a screech of tires, then a sound she can only describe as a wet, heavy thud. She remembers Liam’s laughter stopping. She remembers turning her head just in time to see a young woman’s body lift into the air and land on the pavement, twisted and still. The driver didn’t stop.

F. did not know the woman. But she cannot stop seeing her. The woman was wearing a red scarf, the same shade F.’s mother used to wear to Friday prayers. In the days after, F. could not enter the backyard. She told her employer she had a stomach bug. She would sit in the kitchen instead, watching the children through the glass door, her heart hammering against her ribs. She thought the feeling would pass.

It did not pass.

Now, F. avoids that entire neighborhood. She takes the long way to the grocery store, adding twenty minutes to her trip. She no longer watches the news. The sound of a car horn makes her drop whatever she is holding. Last week, a delivery truck backfired outside her apartment, and F. found herself on the floor of her hallway, her hands over her ears, unable to breathe. Her husband, Ahmed, found her there. He did not know what to do. He brought her a glass of water and stood over her, waiting.

F. has not returned to work. She calls the children’s mother every few days, telling her she is still “unwell.” She misses them—she misses Liam’s sticky hands and the way his sister would hide her favorite toy in F.’s apron pocket. But the thought of stepping into that yard, of pushing a swing, of hearing that same creak of the metal chain, makes her feel as though she is drowning. She has nightmares nearly every night. In them, the woman in the red scarf is standing in F.’s bedroom, her body bent at an impossible angle. The woman never speaks. She just points at F.

F. has lost twelve pounds. She cannot eat. Food tastes like dust. She spends most of her days sitting in the dark living room, her rosary beads wrapped around her fingers, counting prayers she cannot finish. Ahmed has started cooking for her, but she pushes the food around the plate. She feels guilty. He is a good man. He does not understand why she cannot “just forget it.” She does not understand either.

She tells me she feels hollow, like a bell that has been rung too hard and will not stop vibrating. She is irritable with Ahmed, snapping at him for small things—the way he chews, the volume of the television. Afterward, she cries. She has not left the apartment in nine days. She does not want to see anyone. She does not want to be seen.

F. has never been to therapy before. In her culture, she says, you take your problems to God, not to a stranger. But she came because she is tired. She is tired of being afraid. She is tired of the red scarf. She is tired of feeling like a stranger in her own body. She sits across from me, her hands now still, and she asks, quietly, if I think she will ever feel safe again. She does not wait for an answer.
